Dahomey. The historical kingdom and French colonial territory in West Africa lasted from the seventeenth century until decolonization in nineteen-sixty. The nation renamed itself Benin in nineteen-seventy-five under the revolutionary government of Mathieu Kérékou, honoring the Benin Empire, a powerful pre-colonial West African state centered in what is now Nigeria. The renaming reflected anti-colonial pride and a broader pan-African reorientation toward celebrating indigenous African heritage over colonial nomenclature.

The Dahomey Kingdom, flourishing from around sixteen twenty-five to nineteen hundred, was a powerful West African state known for its military prowess, its famous female warrior regiments, and its involvement in the Atlantic slave trade. France colonized Dahomey in stages, making it a French protectorate by eighteen-ninety-four and a full colony by nineteen hundred, integrating it into French West Africa. Dahomey gained independence in nineteen-sixty as a French-speaking republic, but the name itself perpetuated colonial associations with the old kingdom.

In nineteen-seventy-five, President Mathieu Kérékou instituted a socialist revolution and renamed the country Benin after the historical Benin Empire of Nigeria. The Benin Empire was a powerful medieval and early-modern state spanning the thirteenth through nineteenth centuries, centered in what is now southern Nigeria, not geographically in present-day Benin. The name change was part of a broader post-colonial gesture to reclaim African heritage. Kérékou's government also changed the capital from Porto-Novo to Cotonou, symbolizing a complete break with the colonial era. In renaming itself, the nation honored an ancient African superpower and asserted its own sovereignty.
